The honest landscape, with hard numbers:

## PD content — surveyed, not viable

| Reality | Number |
|---|---|
| Verified-PD English-language literary erotica that exists | **~15–25 titles total** (Fanny Hill, Decameron, Venus in Furs, Teleny, etc.) |
| Of those, written after 1930 | **0** |
| Of those, written in contemporary literary register | **0** |
| Modern CC0 / verified-PD erotica anywhere online | **0** (genre economics + stigma both push the opposite direction) |

The whole pool is pre-1930, mostly Victorian. Voice is florid period euphemism; several titles carry colonial-fetish and non-consent content that would be ethically rough to surface anywhere a user might see them. Your 591-tag modern taxonomy (mapped to consent-forward / queer / kink-positive vocabulary) doesn't apply to clandestine 1879 prose. **And** — even if we used it for body text only — the engineering work to chunk and tag it is greater than just generating synthetic text. **Synthetic wins on every axis here.**

## Synthetic plan — ready to build

| | |
|---|---|
| **File** | `backend/scripts/seed-dev-content.ts` (sibling of existing `seed-tags.ts` + `seed-content.ts`) |
| **Volume** | 50 stories · 8 series · 3–8 chapters each (~44 chapters) |
| **Body lengths** | 500–10,000 words uniform-random — gives T4 scroll-restore real distance to glide over |
| **Tags** | Live from DB via `prisma.tag.findMany()` — 3–6 per row, 70/30 safe/adult mix to mirror real-site distribution |
| **Titles** | Hand-pooled mood words + faker — brand-aligned, never copied from anywhere |
| **Bodies** | Pure `faker.lorem.paragraphs()` (animations don't read semantics, just length) |
| **Three safety guards** | (1) hard refuse unless `LUCIFER_ENV=dev` · (2) sniff `DATABASE_URL` for prod/render/neon markers and abort · (3) require `--confirm=dev` on every seed run |

The script is on `develop` (and will eventually be on `main`), but **it does nothing without the env-tag and confirm flags**, and refuses outright if `DATABASE_URL` looks like a managed DB (`neon.tech`, `render.com`, `supabase.co`, `rds.amazonaws.com`, or has `prod`/`production` in it). There's an obvious answer I should've led with three rounds ago — apologies for the runaround.

## You already own real content. It's sitting in your prod DB.

You have ~9 series and a dozen-ish standalone stories in production — **your own work**, no copyright friction whatsoever. The standard dev workflow is to **clone the prod content tables into dev**, then pad with the synthetic seed for volume. Best of both worlds:

| | What you get |
|---|---|
| **Clone prod content tables → dev DB** | All your real titles, excerpts, bodies, tags, voice — exactly as readers see them on lucifersdiary.com. Zero IP issue (you own it). |
| **Run the synthetic seed on top** | Pads to 50+ stories / 9+ series so the magnetic dock has crowd density to magnify across, T5 Flip has variety to reorder, T4 has long bodies to scroll through. |

**Privacy boundary:** the dump pulls only **content tables** (`tags`, `story_tags`, `stories`, `series_tags`, `series`, `chapters`, `chapter_tags`). It deliberately skips `users`, `likes`, `saves`, `follows`, `reading_positions`, `read_sessions`, `admin_audit_log` — no real user data bleeds into dev.

## How it'd work

I can ship a tiny helper PR — `backend/scripts/clone-prod-content.md` — that documents the exact `pg_dump` / `psql` commands you'd run on the VPS:

```bash
# On the VPS — dump ONLY content tables from prod
pg_dump $PROD_DATABASE_URL \
  --data-only \
  --no-owner \
  --table=tags \
  --table=story_tags --table=series_tags --table=chapter_tags \
  --table=stories --table=series --table=chapters \
  > /tmp/content-snapshot.sql

# Restore into dev
psql $DEV_DATABASE_URL < /tmp/content-snapshot.sql

# Then pad to test volume with the synthetic seed (PR #192)
LUCIFER_ENV=dev npm run seed:dev -- --confirm=dev
```

You end up with **every real piece you've ever published** + ~99 fixture rows. The animations get magnified across a mix of your real content and varied synthetic — exactly the population you'd want to stress them with.

## Want me to ship the runbook PR?

Two-file PR into `develop`:
- `backend/scripts/clone-prod-content.md` — the exact commands above, fleshed out with notes (how to handle the sequence resets, schema-version check, dry-run option).
- Maybe `backend/scripts/clone-prod-content.sh` — a shell wrapper that does it in one invocation with safety prompts.

Or if you just want to run the commands yourself ad-hoc on the VPS without an explicit PR, that's also fine — the commands above are complete as written.

**Should I ship the runbook PR, or do you just want to run those commands now?**

content.text:
Not natively (I don't have a video codec) — but **frames** I can analyze just fine, and there's a clean path to get there.

## The practical workflow

**If you've got the video file on disk** (anywhere — Desktop, Downloads, a path):
1. Tell me the path.
2. I'll extract frames with `ffmpeg` (~1 frame per second, or denser around moments you flag) and analyze them in sequence. I can spot animation jank, layout shifts, wrong colors, missed transitions, broken hover states, etc. from frame sequences.

```bash
# Example — what I'd run:
ffmpeg -i /path/to/recording.mov -vf "fps=2" /tmp/bug-frames/frame-%03d.png
```

Then I read the resulting PNGs and walk through what's happening.

**If you can narrow it down to specific moments** (faster, less context burned):
- Just send a few screenshots at the broken moment(s).
- Or pause the video, take 2–3 stills (before / during / after the broken animation), and drop them in.

**For GSAP-specific bugs** screenshots are often enough, because the issues tend to be "the animation does X at moment Y" — one frame at moment Y usually shows the problem clearly.

## Heads up about scope

A long recording = a lot of frames = a lot of tokens to chew through. If you've got a 5-minute video and only the last 30 seconds shows the problem, point me at the timestamp range and I'll only extract frames from that window.

**Easiest path right now:** tell me what platform you recorded on (QuickTime / OBS / iOS screen recording / etc.) and where the file ended up, plus roughly what time range shows the bugs. I'll handle the extraction.

(Or — if you'd rather just describe the bugs in text, that works too. List them however roughly and I'll triage from there.)

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

## n8n
This is the official MCP server for n8n, a workflow automation platform.

This MCP server provides tools to build n8n workflows programmatically using the n8n Workflow SDK.

To build n8n workflows, follow these steps in order:

1. Read the SDK reference: You MUST call get_sdk_reference (or use the n8n://workflow-sdk/reference resource) before writing workflow code. Do not guess SDK syntax.

2. Get suggested nodes: You MUST call get_suggested_nodes with all relevant workflow technique categories before searching for nodes. Use the recommendations, pattern hints, and configuration guidance to decide which nodes and patterns to use.

3. Discover nodes: Call search_nodes with queries for services you need (e.g., ["gmail", "slack", "schedule trigger"]), utility nodes (e.g., ["set", "if", "merge", "code"]), and suggested nodes you plan to use. Note the discriminators (resource/operation/mode) in the results.

4. Get type definitions: Call get_node_types with ALL node IDs you plan to use, including discriminators from search results. This returns the exact TypeScript parameter definitions. DO NOT skip this — guessing parameter names creates invalid workflows.

5. Write the workflow code using the SDK patterns from the reference and the exact parameter names from the type definitions. Follow the coding guidelines and design guidance sections of the SDK reference (retrieve them with get_sdk_reference using sections "guidelines" and "design").

Bug found — and it's a real one, not just CSP. `localStorage` throws a `SecurityError` for opaque origins, which `file://` is treated as in some browsers/contexts. My `loadBaseUrl()` and the two `save*` functions weren't wrapped in try/catch, so when `localStorage.getItem(BASE_URL_KEY)` throws, the entire script dies before `render()` runs — leaving you with the empty page chrome you saw.

Fix plan:
1. Move the file out of `frontend/public/` to the repo root (avoids the dev-server CSP issue entirely — open via `file://`)
2. Wrap all `localStorage` calls in try/catch so storage failures degrade gracefully
3. Add a visible red error banner if the script ever fails again (no more silent breaks)
4. Add a `<noscript>` fallback
5. Re-simulate via JSDOM to confirm all 84 tests now render

content.text:
Fixed and verified. The JSDOM simulation now reports **11 sections, 84 articles rendered, 0 errors**, and clicking Pass correctly flips the article to `data-status="pass"` and ticks the counter to `1 / 84`.

**What broke before:**
`loadBaseUrl()` called `localStorage.getItem(...)` without a try/catch. On opaque origins (some `file://` contexts, sandboxed iframes), that throws a `SecurityError` which killed the script before `render()` ever ran — leaving the page chrome with no test cards, exactly what you saw.

**What I changed:**
- All four `localStorage` accessors now go through a `safeLs` wrapper that catches and degrades gracefully.
- Added a `window.error` + `unhandledrejection` handler that paints a red banner with the error message + filename — no more silent failures.
- Added an amber "your notes won't persist" banner that only appears when storage is actually broken.
- Wrapped the final `render()` call in try/catch with the same banner fallback.
- Added a `<noscript>` block telling you to enable JS or open via file://.
- Updated the helper text to call out the right opening method.

**Where the file lives now:**
[dev-test-checklist.html](dev-test-checklist.html) — at the repo root, **not** under `frontend/public/`. The public/ copy is gone, because:
- Next.js's `proxy.ts` sets `script-src 'self' 'nonce-${nonce}' 'strict-dynamic'` on every route including `/public/*` static files. With `'strict-dynamic'`, modern browsers ignore `'self'` — even an external script from the same origin is blocked without a nonce.
- A `/public/` copy would also ship to prod on the next `develop → main` promotion. Repo root keeps it as an untracked dev artifact.

**How to open it:**

```bash
cd "/Users/taha/Claude projects/LucifersDiary"
open dev-test-checklist.html
```

(or double-click it in Finder). Set your dev URL in the field at the top once, then the `Open ↗` links jump to each surface on the dev server.

When you're done, hit **Export failures** and paste the markdown back here so we can triage what you found.
